REL12-BP04 Test resilience using chaos engineering
Chaos engineering injects controlled faults into a system to verify
    that it withstands and recovers from real-world disruptions. Running
    these experiments regularly, in or close to production, builds
    confidence that recovery mechanisms work.
Desired outcome:
You verify workload resilience regularly through fault injection
        experiments and injection of unexpected load.
You combine chaos engineering with resilience testing that
        validates known, expected behavior during an event.
Your experiments run both inside the delivery pipeline and
        outside deployments, under real-world conditions and load.
Successful experiments become automated regression tests that
        guard resilience over time.
Common anti-patterns:
Teams design for resilience but never verify how the whole
        workload behaves when faults occur.
Experiments never run under real-world conditions or expected
        load.
Experiments are not treated as code or maintained through the
        development cycle.
Chaos experiments run only in the pipeline, or only outside it,
        but not both.
Teams ignore past post-incident analyses when choosing which
        faults to inject.
Benefits of establishing this best
    practice:
Recovery procedures are proven against real faults, not assumed
        to work.
Hidden weaknesses surface in a controlled setting where you can
        address them safely.
Alerting and notification paths are validated as part of each
        experiment.
Resilience improves continually as experiments become permanent
        regression tests.
Level of risk exposed if this best practice
    is not established:
Medium
Implementation guidance
The
Principles of Chaos Engineering
define the discipline as experimenting
      on a system to build confidence in its ability to withstand
      turbulent conditions in production. Focus experiments on
known-unknowns
(things you are aware of but
      do not understand) and
unknown-unknowns
(things you are neither aware of nor understand). Discover the
      failure modes your design did not anticipate while keeping the
      blast radius small and controlled.
Steady state
is a measurable output that
      indicates normal behavior, such as processing 300 transactions per
      second at a 99 percent success rate with a 500 ms round-trip time.
      A
hypothesis
predicts that steady state will
      hold under a specific fault, because the workload's mitigations
      handle it. Define both before you inject a fault: the steady-state
      metric is your baseline, and the hypothesis is the claim the
      experiment tests. Post-incident analyses are a strong source of
      both the faults worth injecting and the metrics worth watching.
Guardrails keep experiments safe. Define stop conditions on the
      metrics that represent steady state and on the components you are
      injecting faults into, so an experiment halts automatically before
      it causes unacceptable impact. Include a synthetic monitor, or
      user canary, as a proxy for customer experience. Simulate faults
      in a non-production environment first to confirm that stop
      conditions activate and observability catches exceptions, then
      move toward production, where real load reveals behavior that no
      lower environment reproduces. Run first experiments during
      off-peak hours, and use synthetic traffic against control and
      experimental deployments when customer traffic poses too much
      risk.
AWS Fault Injection Service running experiments across resource types
The preceding figure shows
AWS Fault Injection Service (AWS FIS)
, a managed service for
      running experiments inside or outside your delivery pipeline. AWS
      FIS introduces faults across resource types including Amazon EC2,
      Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, Amazon RDS, Amazon DynamoDB, AWS Lambda,
      Amazon S3, and networking services. Fault types include:
Instance termination
Forced failover
CPU and memory stress
Throttling
Latency
Packet loss
Full-AZ interruption scenarios
Network disruptions between AZs, VPCs, or specific services
Use multi-step experiment workflows to sequence actions and model
      cascading failures. Use cross-account experiments to run scenarios
      against resources in multiple accounts from a central account. The
experiment templates library
provides pre-built scenarios for common
      resilience patterns such as AZ failover, Region failover, and
      dependency failure.
AWS Resilience Hub
recommends and can trigger FIS experiments
      based on resilience assessment findings. AWS FIS integrates with
      Amazon CloudWatch alarms for stop conditions that roll back an
      experiment on unexpected impact. Open-source tools such as Chaos
      Toolkit, Chaos Mesh, and Litmus Chaos, and commercial tools such
      as Gremlin, extend the range of faults. AWS FIS coordinates
      workflows across several of these tools.
Continuous resilience flywheel for chaos engineering
The experiment loop follows the continuous resilience flywheel in
      the preceding figure: define steady state, form a hypothesis, run
      the experiment, verify the result, and improve the design before
      running again. When a workload survives an experiment, keep it as
      an automated regression test in your systems development lifecycle
      and delivery pipeline, so a future change cannot silently
      reintroduce the weakness. A fault design or a failed experiment
      can leave a workload in an unexpected state. Give every experiment
      a rollback path, such as an AWS FIS post action, and document it
      in a playbook.
Implementation steps
Determine which faults to experiment
            with:
Assess your workload design for resilience
            and list each element intended to maintain it, along with
            the faults it mitigates. Draw on critical dependencies, past
            events, known issues, and compliance requirements. The
            Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) process gives you
            a framework for component-level analysis of failures and
            their impact. Start with the
AWS FIS experiment templates library
for pre-built
            scenarios covering common resilience patterns, and review
AWS Resilience Hub
assessment recommendations for
            targeted experiments specific to your application.
Prioritize each fault:
Categorize faults as high, medium, or low priority using
            frequency and impact. Estimate frequency from historical
            data for this workload, or from similar workloads when none
            exists. Weigh impact by the scope of the fault and the
            workload's purpose, and use post-incident analyses to ground
            both estimates.
Define steady state and form a
            hypothesis:
Confirm the workload is healthy, then
            define steady state as a measurable output such as a success
            rate and latency percentile. Write a hypothesis stating
            that, given a specific fault, the workload maintains steady
            state because of specific mitigations. Specify the fault
            type and the mitigating controls.
Run the experiment with
            guardrails:
Inject the fault using
AWS FIS
actions or custom actions defined in
AWS Systems Manager documents
. Set
stop conditions
on steady-state and component metrics,
            include a
synthetic monitor
as a user proxy, and run in a non-production
            environment before production. Inform operations,
            reliability, and support teams before you begin.
Verify the hypothesis:
Compare the measured output against the steady-state metrics
            you defined. Focus on customer-facing signals such as
            server-side error rates and failed requests, supplemented by
            the direct consequence of the fault. If steady state held,
            the hypothesis is confirmed.
Improve the design and
            re-run:
If steady state was not maintained,
            investigate how to strengthen the design, applying the best
            practices of the Reliability pillar and resources in the
AWS Builders' Library
. After implementing changes, run
            the experiment again to confirm they work.
Automate and run experiments
            regularly:
Once a workload meets a hypothesis,
            automate the experiment as a regression test in your
            delivery pipeline and run it on a regular cadence. Use FIS
scheduled experiments
to run tests on a recurring schedule
            without requiring pipeline integration for every execution.
            Include fault injection in your game days so teams rehearse
            the response as if a real event occurred.
Capture and store
            results:
Persist each experiment's results with
            enough context to analyze trends later, including time,
            workload, and conditions. Use
experiment logging with AWS FIS
alongside dashboards and
            recorded observations.
